title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access masks by PowerShell and wsmprovhost under user pbeesly
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as pbeesly) opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff — PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-class rights used for memory dumping, with a short UNKNOWN-module call trace. The same activity repeated on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z from C:\windows\system32\wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, PowerShell remoting host, user pbeesly) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff, call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll. Windows Security corroborates: 4656 handle requests to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff by powershell.exe on scranton (SubjectUserName pbeesly) and by wsmprovhost.exe on nashua (SubjectUserName pbeesly), followed by 4663 read (0x10) events. This is not the baseline pattern: the dominant LSASS accessor is svchost.exe with 0x1000 (293 of 326 events), and the only other high-mask accessors are Defender MsMpEng.exe and Azure CollectGuestLogs.exe. The pbeesly session on scranton is independently malicious (Invoke-Exfil script, PsExec64 to \\NASHUA with cleartext password, davclnt.dll WebDAV staging to 192.168.0.4, hidden encoded PowerShell), so the LSASS full-access handles are credential dumping in the course of that intrusion.

title: SAM_SERVER handle with 0xF003F requested by lsass.exe on scranton during the intrusion
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, Security 4656 events show handles requested to ObjectName 'SAM' (Object Server 'Security Account Manager', Object Type SAM_SERVER) with AccessMask 0xf003f (DELETE, READ_CONTROL, WRITE_DAC, WRITE_OWNER, ConnectToServer, ShutdownServer, InitializeServer, CreateDomain, EnumerateDomains, LookupDomain) at 03:19:21-03:19:22Z and 03:20:46Z, plus handles to \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Services\SamSs at 03:19:10Z. The requesting process is C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe under SubjectUserName SCRANTON$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3e7), i.e. the SAM service itself, which is the normal owner of these objects — no non-lsass process was seen reading the SAM hive. No reg save / hive export command lines were found (only dsregcmd.exe and sc.exe start pushtoinstall registration matched the reg/save/SAM/ntds pattern), and no SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive files were created on disk (only Prefetch .pf files matched). The timing inside the pbeesly intrusion window keeps this worth noting, but the actor and access path are the legitimate SAM server, so I cannot attribute SAM dumping.

title: No NTDS.dit access or copy observed
summary: No evidence of NTDS.dit theft. File-creation events matching ntds/.dit/.dmp returned only two Windows Error Reporting crash dumps (C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\WER\Temp\WER51F5.tmp.dmp and WER5437.tmp.dmp), and no process command line contained ntds, vssadmin, shadow or procdump. The domain controller newyork.dmevals.local shows only machine-account network logons (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, WEC$, SCRANTON$ type 3) and no directory-service replication access was observed.

title: LSA secrets not accessed by any non-system process
summary: The only LSASS accessors with elevated rights were the malicious PowerShell/wsmprovhost handles (covered under T1003.001); all other LSASS handle sources are baseline (svchost.exe 289 events at 0x1000, Azure AntimalwareConfig.exe 15, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 13, plus wininit/csrss/services). Registry modifications touching SECURITY/LSA paths were limited to HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 (5 events) and benign CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc / CredentialGuard service keys; no SECURITY\Policy\Secrets access was observed.

title: Cached domain credential store (SECURITY\Cache) not read by attacker tooling
summary: Registry writes to HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 (5 events) are the only cached-credential-related modifications and are consistent with normal logon cache maintenance; the remaining 'Cache' matches are unrelated (NetworkList NLA cache, TaskCache, AppContainer Internet Settings cache). No process was observed reading the SECURITY\Cache hive, and the LSASS access that could expose DCC2 hashes is the same PowerShell/wsmprovhost activity already reported under T1003.001.

title: No DCSync / DRSUAPI replication abuse observed
summary: No process command line or PowerShell script block contained drsuapi, lsadump, dcsync or Invoke-Mimikatz. The only PowerShell script blocks on the DC newyork.dmevals.local are DSC resource modules (xDNSServerAddress, xStorage, MSFT_ScriptResourceStrings) and AD cmdlet help text, all running as SYSTEM. Directory replication access was not observed on newyork.dmevals.local.

title: netsh trace packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure Network Watcher agent telemetry, not adversary sniffing
summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:19:17 UTC the only packet-capture activity in the whole dataset appeared on scranton.dmevals.local: netsh.exe was launched as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (LogonId 0x3E7) with 'netsh.exe trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"'. Both Sysmon EID 1 and Security EID 4688 show the parent as C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (PID 3180, '/service'), and the capture was stopped 7 seconds later by the same parent ('netsh.exe trace stop'). The surrounding activity is the Azure guest-agent/Network Watcher lifecycle: NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service at 03:19:13, logman.exe stop/create/start of GAEvents and RTEvents writing to C:\WindowsAzure\Logs\*.etl, and NetworkWatcherAgent.exe Test/Install/Start /service /autoStart at 03:20:41-42. No third-party or offensive capture tooling was found: no pktmon, windump, tcpdump, rawcap, dumpcap, Wireshark or promiscuous-mode command lines in Sysmon EID 1 or Security 4688, no capture-related driver/image loads (pktmon/npcap/wpcap/ndiscap) in Sysmon EID 6, and no PowerShell capture scripting (4104 check C047 zero hits). The 7045 service installs in windows.other are javamtsup.exe and repeated PSEXESVC.exe (pbeesly) on nashua, unrelated to packet capture. Zeek data (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and shows only ordinary conn/ssl/dns/smb/kerberos logs with no capture-specific record type. Conclusion: T1040 is not evidenced as attacker behaviour; the netsh trace is legitimate Azure platform network diagnostics.

title: pbeesly PowerShell/wsmprovhost requests full-access (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) handles to lsass.exe on scranton and nashua
summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16Z (23:05:16 -04:00) the account DMEVALS\pbeesly, running as C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe (PID 0xba0, logon 0x372E81), requested two handles to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe on scranton.dmevals.local with AccessMask 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff — including 'Read from process memory', 'Write to process memory', 'Perform virtual memory operation' and 'Duplicate handle into or out of process'. At 03:09:29Z the same account requested a 0x1f3fff handle to lsass.exe on nashua.dmevals.local from C:\Windows\System32\wsmprovhost.exe (PID 0x1e28, logon 0x85AAD2), i.e. over a PowerShell remoting session. These are the only non-system, non-AV LSASS handle requests in the dataset (the other 4656 lsass hits are CollectGuestLogs.exe, MsMpEng.exe and lsass.exe itself under machine accounts). Full-access process handles to LSASS from PowerShell are the classic credential-API-hooking / memory-read pattern used to extract logon credentials. No 4104 script block containing lsass/minidump/sekurlsa/hook strings was found, so the exact tooling is not visible in PowerShell logging.

title: Suspicious .scr and python.exe payloads on scranton/nashua open full-access (0x1FFFFF) handles to conhost/cmd/powershell
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr (PID 8524, launched by explorer.exe as DMEVALS\pbeesly at 02:55:56Z, SHA256 0DF38A55D940F498478EB03683C94D4584236E100125B526A67650BA54DF4AE4) opened 0x1FFFFF handles to conhost.exe and cmd.exe at 02:56:04Z and 02:57:12Z; the file was later wiped with sdelete64.exe at 03:02:04Z. On nashua.dmevals.local, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe (PID 2172, spawned by another C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, user DMEVALS\pbeesly) opened 0x1FFFFF handles to powershell.exe (03:15:48Z) and cmd.exe (03:16:40Z). Full-access handles to console/shell processes are consistent with input capture / process injection, but no keyboard-hook, GetAsyncKeyState or keylogger registry artifacts were observed, so the capture mechanism itself is not proven.

title: No keylogger artifacts: no keyboard-hook registry writes or keylogging script blocks
summary: The 17,541 Sysmon registry-value-set (event 13) events are dominated by W32Time, DeliveryOptimization, UserAssist, BAM and ContentDeliveryManager keys; the 1,357 hits for Keyboard/keylog/Services registry paths are ordinary service configuration writes (e.g. svchost.exe writing HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\Config\LastKnownGoodTime). No 4104 script block contained GetAsyncKeyState, keylog or SetWindowsHookEx. No keylogger persistence or configuration key was observed.

title: No GUI input capture (credential prompt spoofing) observed
summary: No evidence of fake credential dialogs or GUI input capture was found in the retrieved data; the only GUI-adjacent activity is the .scr payload's full-access handles to conhost/cmd, which is reported under T1056 rather than as GUI prompt capture.

title: No web portal capture: no IIS/wwwroot/aspx writes or login-page HTTP activity
summary: Checks for file writes to wwwroot/inetpub/.aspx, IIS/appcmd/w3wp command lines, PowerShell referencing wwwroot/inetpub/appcmd, and HTTP URLs containing login/auth/signin all returned zero hits, so no web portal credential-capture activity was observed.

title: No brute-force authentication activity observed; credential theft was done by dumping lsass, not by guessing
summary: Across the whole windows.security window (2020-05-02T02:55:25Z..03:28:09Z, 4 hosts) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events, zero 4771/4776 failure statuses and zero 4740 lockouts. The only 4776 in the dataset is a successful NTLM validation (Status 0x0) for pbeesly on newyork.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:20:40-04:00. Successful 4624 logons are dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SCRANTON$ 37, NASHUA$ 25) and pbeesly (20, type 3), consistent with normal service/network logons. No authentication-failure burst exists to support a brute-force hypothesis.

title: No password guessing: zero 4625 events on any host
summary: The count of event.code:4625 in windows.security is 0 for the entire collection window, so there is no repeated failed authentication against any account or host that would indicate password guessing. The credential access that did occur on scranton.dmevals.local was memory-based (lsass handle with 0x1fffff), not password guessing.

title: No offline cracking tooling or hash-dump artifacts; lsass access by PowerShell/wsmprovhost is credential dumping, not cracking
summary: No hashcat/john/cracking binaries appear in the 447 process-create events, and no .pot/.hash/ntds.dit output files appear among 1649 file-create events. However, the lsass process-access stack shows two non-system processes opening lsass with dump-grade access: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, spawned by control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter with a hidden -ep bypass IEX-from-bitmap loader) opened lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff then 0x1fffff on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, user pbeesly, PowerShell remoting) opened lsass with 0x1f3fff on nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:09:29Z. Security 4656/4663 corroborate the same handles (0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe). The 10 SAM_SERVER 4656 events are all lsass.exe itself under SCRANTON$ at 23:19-23:20 local, coinciding with a system restart (wininit/csrss re-opening lsass at 03:19:09Z), i.e. benign. The 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff lsass handles are the credential-theft step that would feed offline cracking, but no cracking itself was observed.

title: No password spraying; the only explicit-credential logons are PsExec reuse of the already-known pbeesly password
summary: There are no 4625 failures, so no spray pattern exists. The 15 4648 explicit-credential events are: 9 for pbeesly (5 on scranton.dmevals.local targeting NASHUA from 10.0.1.6, 4 on nashua.dmevals.local from C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe), plus DWM-1/DWM-2/UMFD-0/UMFD-1/UMFD-2/SCRANTON$ from winlogon/wininit/taskhostw (normal session setup). The pbeesly 4648s pair with PsExec64.exe being run on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:11:18Z with the cleartext password on the command line (\\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe), followed by python.exe launching on nashua.dmevals.local under PSEXESVC.exe at 03:11:40Z. This is reuse of a single already-obtained credential for lateral movement, not spraying across many accounts.

title: No credential stuffing: no failed logons and no multi-account credential list use
summary: Credential stuffing requires many failed authentications from a list of stolen credentials; windows.security contains 0 events with event.code:4625 and no 4771/4776 failure statuses, and the 218 type-3 network logons involve only machine accounts plus pbeesly. The single account used with explicit credentials is pbeesly, so there is no evidence of stuffing a credential list against the hosts.

title: PowerShell steganography loader on scranton exported certificate private keys (PFX) and opened LSASS with full access
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (PID 2976, parent control.exe) that decoded a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX'd it. The session then ran discovery, persistence steps, accesschk, and a Get-PrivateKeys function that enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports each certificate with a private key to a random .pfx in the user's Downloads folder (password 'saribas'). At 03:04:57 a file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx was created by powershell.exe and at 03:08:51 the same file was deleted (Sysmon 23) by powershell.exe. At 03:05:16 the same PowerShell process (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (full access) with an UNKNOWN call trace, i.e. direct credential-store access from the attacker's PowerShell. This is credential material theft (certificate private keys usable for authentication / MFA-bypass via certificate-based logon) rather than interception of an MFA provider; no smart-card/MFA provider tampering was observed. Related: on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM PowerShell) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29, and pbeesly credentials were used explicitly via PSEXESVC.exe (4648, target localhost) at 23:11:40 local, consistent with reuse of the stolen account.

title: Smart-card / crypto registry and service activity is Windows baseline, not MFA interception
summary: The only smart-card/crypto-related registry writes were made by core Windows processes during normal boot/startup on scranton.dmevals.local: smss.exe setting Cryptography\Calais symbolic links, taskhostw.exe writing CertificateTemplateCache timestamps, and services.exe writing an MUICache entry for SCardSvr.dll ('Smart Card'). No smart-card or MFA provider DLL was registered, replaced or configured by a non-system process, and no script block referenced smart-card/MFA APIs (the three 4104 hits were unrelated module/help text and an exfiltration function). The 7045 service installs were javamtsup.exe and repeated PSEXESVC.exe (PsExec lateral movement by pbeesly), not MFA-provider tampering. LSASS handle opens with 0x1000/0x1400 by svchost.exe, AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe are routine security/telemetry reads.

title: No forced-authentication (T1187) activity observed; LSASS reads and SMB traffic are benign system/administrative behaviour
summary: Hunting for T1187 on 2020-05-02 02:55–03:28Z found no coercion artefacts. The six 4663 events on lsass.exe objects are all AccessMask 0x10 (read) by machine accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$) via C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\CollectGuestLogs.exe and MsMpEng.exe, plus one by pbeesly via powershell.exe — routine Azure guest-agent/AV/administrative reads, not credential dumping or forced auth. The three shortcut files created (Sysmon 11) are Explorer 'Recent' .lnk files for pbeesly and a StartUp\hostui.lnk written by powershell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local; the hostui.lnk is part of a local persistence chain (hostui.txt dropped from SysinternalsSuite, Invoke-Persistence -PersistStep 1/2, then hostui.bat -> powershell Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas) and points to a local path, not a UNC/WebDAV resource, so it does not force outbound NTLM. SMB (Sysmon 3, port 445) traffic goes only to internal addresses 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6 and a link-local IPv6 address, and 5145 IPC$ access shows pbeesly using samr/svcctl/PSEXESVC against newyork and nashua from 10.0.1.4 — lateral PsExec-style administration, not authentication coercion to an attacker host. No WebDAV/NTLM/Responder script blocks were found (C104 zero hits).

On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice within 31 ms at 2020-05-02T03:05:16 (GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff, call trace ending in UNKNOWN modules), and on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29. These are the only high-access LSASS handles in the window; the other 317 LSASS accesses are svchost/Azure agent reads at 0x1000/0x1400. The surrounding activity on scranton is hands-on-keyboard by user pbeesly: accesschk.exe (03:04:34), sdelete64.exe against Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip (03:03:14/03:03:33), csc.exe/cvtres.exe compiling from C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Local\Temp (03:08:03), PsExec64.exe to \\NASHUA with the cleartext password for dmevals\pbeesly (03:11:18), and hidden encoded PowerShell plus 'Get-ItemPropertyValue HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft ... | Invoke-Expression' spawned from hostui.exe (03:21:27). However, nothing retrieved shows exploitation of a vulnerable service/application to obtain these handles: no crash-then-child pattern, no service/app process spawning children (parents are services.exe, svchost.exe, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, Azure agents), no Mimikatz/sekurlsa script blocks (4104 search returned none), and the LSASS call traces point to PowerShell/.NET rather than an exploited process. Credential access is real but the T1212 exploitation vector is unconfirmed.
title: LSASS accessed with full-access rights by PowerShell (scranton) and wsmprovhost (nashua) during a pbeesly intrusion — no exploitation of a vulnerable service observed
No web session cookie theft observed; browser cookie-store activity on scranton is MicrosoftEdge.exe's own profile I/O
summary: Hunting for T1539 across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55–03:28Z) found no evidence of cookie-store theft. The only events touching browser cookie/profile paths are on scranton.dmevals.local under user pbeesly, and every one of them is performed by MicrosoftEdge.exe itself: Sysmon 23 file-delete of Edge AC\Temp ~DF*.TMP files at 03:18:33, Sysmon 11 creation of ...\MicrosoftEdge\User\Default\DataStore\_TempTestAccess.txt at 03:21:05, and Sysmon 11 creation of Edge RecoveryStore .dat and further ~DF*.TMP files at 03:21:05–03:21:06. A query for any non-Edge process touching *microsoftedge*, *google*, *mozilla* or *cookies* paths returned only svchost.exe creating C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\...\AC\INetCookies and Prefetch GOOGLEUPDATE.EXE-B95715F5.pf entries — normal OS/updater behaviour. No Sysmon 10 process-access to chrome/firefox/msedge/iexplore images (check C114, zero hits), no security 4663 object access to Cookies/Login Data/Web Data/Edge/Chrome/Mozilla paths, and no PowerShell 4104 script block referencing cookies, Login Data, sqlite or browser profile paths. The C112 'Cookies/Login Data/Web Data' aggregate hits were false positives from the substring 'DataStore' in GroupPolicy and Edge paths plus lastalive*.dat, not browser credential stores. Separately, the same window does contain clearly malicious activity on scranton.dmevals.local by pbeesly (Invoke-ScreenCapture/Keystroke-Check script block, Invoke-Exfil staging to \\192.168.0.4\webdav, sdelete64 wiping C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr) and PsExec-delivered C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local, but none of that activity reads or exfiltrates browser cookie databases, so it is not T1539.

title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports every LocalMachine certificate to .pfx on SCRANTON
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script block (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) at 2020-05-01T23:04:56-04:00 that defines Get-PrivateKeys: it builds a SecureString from the hardcoded plaintext password "saribas", enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint into $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx. One second later Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe. This is private-key/certificate theft staged for exfiltration (the same host then ran Invoke-Exfil compressing Downloads and copying it to a WebDAV share).

title: Recursive user-profile sweep for password/login-named files archived to Draft.Zip on SCRANTON
summary: At 2020-05-01T22:56:17-04:00 on scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly's PowerShell session (PID 5944) ran a script block that recursively enumerates $env:USERPROFILE for documents plus wildcard patterns *psw*, *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *sifr*, *sifer*, *vpn and archives the results with Compress-Archive into $env:APPDATA\Draft.Zip — a classic search of user files for stored credentials. The same session then ran Invoke-Discovery (host/user/AV enumeration) and later Invoke-Exfil, which 7-Zips the Downloads folder and copies it to \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials (cozy / MyCozyPassw0rd!). The 4648 explicit-credential logons by pbeesly to NASHUA over SMB (port 445, source 10.0.1.6) and via PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local show the harvested account being reused for lateral movement.

summary: The 24 Sysmon registry value-set events touching Password/Credential/Winlogon paths are all attributable to Windows components: services.exe (10), svchost.exe (6), winlogon.exe (6), lsass.exe (1) and wininit.exe (1) on scranton/nashua, covering keys such as CredentialGuard\Enabled, CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc_13619b and Winlogon\PasswordExpiryNotification. No reg query/save/export command lines and no 4663 access to SAM/SECURITY/Password objects were found, so no registry credential harvesting is evidenced.

title: SYSVOL/GPO reads are routine machine-account policy refresh, not GPP cpassword harvesting
summary: The 38 5145 SMB accesses to \\*\SYSVOL are gpt.ini, Policies, Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf reads performed by computer accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$) from their own IPs during normal Group Policy refresh; no Groups.xml, cpassword, gpprefdecrypt or AES-key script/command activity was found in PowerShell, Sysmon process or file events.

title: Unsecured credentials: hardcoded plaintext passwords in attacker PowerShell tooling on SCRANTON
summary: Across scranton.dmevals.local the pbeesly PowerShell session (2020-05-01 22:56–23:08) contains multiple hardcoded plaintext secrets in script blocks: "saribas" used as the .pfx export password in Get-PrivateKeys, "lolol" as the 7-Zip archive password in Invoke-Exfil, and "MyCozyPassw0rd!" for the cozy account used to mount \\192.168.0.4\webdav. Combined with the recursive *pass*/*login* file sweep and the certificate export, this is credential collection and staging on a compromised host, followed by SMB/PsExec reuse of pbeesly against nashua.dmevals.local.

summary: On scranton.dmevals.local the user pbeesly ran an interactive PowerShell session that was spawned by a malicious screen-saver (C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr -> cmd.exe -> powershell.exe). At 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z that PowerShell process (PID 2976 / 0xba0) opened handles to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF (Sysmon event 10, call trace ending in UNKNOWN module), and Security 4656 recorded the same handle request with AccessMask 0x1F3FFF listing 'Read from process memory' / 'Perform virtual memory operation'. This is the access pattern of an in-memory credential dump of the LSASS password store. The surrounding session shows the same actor staging SysinternalsSuite, running accesschk, Get-PrivateKeys (exporting certs to .pfx), persistence and screen capture, so the LSASS access is attacker credential theft, not a benign tool.

title: No browser credential-store access observed
summary: Hunting for browser password stores (Chrome 'Login Data'/'Local State', Firefox logins.json/key4.db) found no file creation, no process command line and no object-access audit referencing them on any host. The only file-creation hit was an unrelated INetCookies file written by svchost.exe under the LocalService service profile on scranton.dmevals.local, which is normal Windows behaviour. The actor on scranton did run a recursive file-collection script matching *pass*, *login*, *admin* patterns and compressed the results, but no browser credential database was touched in the retrieved events.

title: No Windows Credential Manager (vault/cmdkey) harvesting observed; LSASS access is covered under T1555
summary: No vaultcmd, cmdkey or Credential-Manager command lines appeared in Sysmon process creation or Security 4688, and no process-access events targeted vaultsvc. The only 'vault/credential' text hits were benign: a Credential Guard configuration message (event 14) on scranton.dmevals.local and PowerShell script blocks containing unrelated words ('validate', 'Get-CommonADParameters'). The rare LSASS handle masks (0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF by PowerShell.exe as pbeesly on scranton) are reported under T1555; the remaining LSASS accessors (svchost.exe with 0x1000/0x101001 via lsm.dll, wininit.exe/csrss.exe at boot, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe and AntimalwareConfig.exe with 0x1400) are normal system/AV behaviour.

title: No password-manager (KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass) access observed
summary: No process creation, process access, file creation (.kdbx/keepass/1password/bitwarden), Security 4688 or PowerShell script block referencing a third-party password manager was found on any of the four hosts. The only credential-adjacent theft in the data is the LSASS handle access on scranton.dmevals.local, which is not a password-manager store.

title: Steganographic PowerShell loader on scranton opened LSASS with full-access mask (0x1FFFFF) — credential access, not auth-process modification
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z, control.exe spawned a hidden, execution-policy-bypass PowerShell (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, High integrity) that decoded a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png via System.Drawing GetPixel and IEX'd it. At 03:05:16Z that same process (SourceProcessGUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — full read/write access consistent with in-memory credential dumping. A second full-access LSASS handle came from wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and a .NET/PowerShell call trace. However, no evidence of authentication-process tampering was found: no 4657 registry changes to LSA/SecurityProviders/Notification Packages/NetworkProvider keys, no 4739, no 5136, no 4657 on NetworkProvider, no lsass image-load of a non-Microsoft module (only lsass.exe loading itself at 03:19:09Z), and no 4688/4104 referencing lsass, procdump, comsvcs, MiniDump or mimikatz. The 289 svchost.exe LSASS accesses (0x1000) and the AntimalwareConfig.exe / WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe accesses (0x1400) are routine. Assessment: credential theft activity is real, but the T1556 family itself is not observed.

title: No domain-controller authentication tampering; 4624/4648 logons are routine machine-account and pbeesly activity
summary: 297 successful logons (4624) are dominated by machine accounts NEWYORK$ (123), SYSTEM (60), SCRANTON$ (37), NASHUA$ (25) and the user pbeesly (30); the 218 network logons (LogonType 3) are loopback/IPv6 machine-account authentications on newyork.dmevals.local. The 15 explicit-credential logons (4648) are pbeesly re-using its own credentials, including four from C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local between 23:11:40 and 23:15:03 local time — consistent with lateral movement by the same actor, not with a backdoor authentication mechanism. No 4657 changes to LSA/SecurityProviders keys, no 4739 policy changes, no 5136 directory-service changes, and no lsass image-load of a third-party module were observed, so no DC authentication-process modification is evidenced.

In the Zeek window (2020-04-30 00:06–00:45Z) host 10.0.1.4 normally sources traffic from MAC 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 (134 conn records, 00:06:38–00:45:00). Starting 00:33:26.283Z a second, different MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 also appears as zeek.orig_l2_addr for the same source IP 10.0.1.4 (44 conn records through 00:45:00.042Z), interleaved with the legitimate MAC on the same destinations and ports (e.g. 10.0.1.6:5985 at 00:33:26, 10.0.1.6:445 at 00:35:25, 10.0.1.6:55121 from 00:36:17). Two distinct L2 addresses claiming one IP simultaneously is the signature of ARP cache poisoning / an on-path attacker, not of a normal NIC change (which would replace, not interleave with, the original MAC). The attacker MAC's traffic is directed at the peer host 10.0.1.6 (NASHUA) on SMB 445, RPC 135, WinRM 5985, HTTP 80 and high port 55121, consistent with interception of that host's traffic.
title: Second MAC address (fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) impersonating IP 10.0.1.4 in parallel with the legitimate NIC MAC — ARP cache poisoning

summary: The poisoned L2 path is used for SMB (445), RPC endpoint mapper (135), WinRM (5985) and HTTP (80) sessions toward 10.0.1.6, i.e. the attacker MAC is positioned on the SMB/RPC path where NTLM relay would occur. Zeek also records NetBIOS name-service broadcasts to 10.0.1.255:137 from 10.0.1.4 (00:35:01.874Z) and from 10.0.1.6 (00:34:51.731Z) — the name-resolution traffic that is poisonable for SMB relay. However, no relayed authentication or poisoned name resolution is directly proven: the SMB sessions to 10.0.0.4 are RSTO (reset/timeout) and the 4624 records show only normal machine-account (type 3) and pbeesly logons. The Windows-side DNS client registry keys (Sysmon 13 *DNSClient*) had zero hits, so no host-level name-resolution tampering is visible.

title: No silver-ticket indicators in TGS requests
summary: The 28 4769 events on newyork.dmevals.local are service-ticket requests for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all with Status 0x0 and AES256 (0x12) encryption, issued to pbeesly and SCRANTON$ from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6. title: No forged web credentials observed; certificate export and WebDAV cookie activity are unrelated to T1606
summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon and windows.powershell (2020-05-02 02:55–03:28Z) there is no evidence of forged web credential material. The 4624 logon-process stack is dominated by Kerberos (217) and Advapi (76) with only 2 User32, 1 NtLmSsp and 1 '-' entries; the User32/NtLmSsp entries are pbeesly interactive (type 10) and network (type 3) logons from 172.18.39.2 on scranton, and the '-' entry is a SYSTEM type-0 boot logon — all normal. The single PowerShell 4104 hit matching token/cookie keywords is the Sysinternals helper function Get-AttributesMask in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1 (SE_GROUP_* token attribute constants), not credential forging. The rare Sysmon process-access masks resolve to svchost/consent/wininit/Explorer/service-host interactions with system processes (e.g. wininit.exe -> lsass.exe 0x1000000, services.exe -> svchost.exe 0x18), which are normal Windows behaviour. Separately, the host does show a real intrusion (pbeesly running discovery, persistence, screen capture, keystroke jobs, sdelete and WebDAV exfiltration to 192.168.0.4), but that is credential/certificate theft and exfiltration, not T1606 web credential forging.

title: WebDAV DavSetCookie invocations are WebClient-service artifacts of the exfiltration script, not forged web cookies
summary: Six rundll32.exe executions of 'davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' ran as DMEVALS\pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:08:50 and 03:10:22-23Z (Sysmon 1 and Security 4688). Their parent is svchost.exe -k LocalService -p -s WebClient, i.e. the Windows WebDAV redirector service, and they coincide with the WebClient service start at 03:08:47Z. This is the normal mechanism by which the WebClient service stores WebDAV auth cookies when the PowerShell Invoke-Exfil function maps \\192.168.0.4\webdav via New-PSDrive — the cookie is being set by the OS for the attacker's own WebDAV share, not a forged/stolen web session cookie being injected. No cookie-file writes to browser stores were found; the only cookie-related file creation is a benign INetCookies package path under the LocalService profile. The underlying exfiltration is malicious, but it is not T1606.001.

title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on SCRANTON, then staged and exfiltrated them
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, in the context of user pbeesly (S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107), a PowerShell script block named Get-PrivateKeys (script block 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) enumerated the entire cert:\LocalMachine store recursively and called Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint, writing each to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. At 03:04:57.460Z Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe (PID 3876) — the same PID that hosted the Get-PrivateKeys script block. Sysmon event 23 confirms the .pfx, .bmp and OfficeSupplies.7z were deleted at 03:08:51. This is deliberate theft of authentication certificates/private keys from the host certificate store, followed by anti-forensic cleanup. The single 4657 modification of HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656 on nashua.dmevals.local was performed by C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe under SYSTEM (NASHUA$) and is unrelated benign certificate-store maintenance, not attacker activity.
